findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: `prisma.credential.update(...)` is called inside `getClient()` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (imports are only getLocation, WEBAPP_URL, HttpError, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse). This will fail type-check/build, and at runtime throws `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce calendar operation, making the Salesforce app completely unusable.

findings.title: Google Calendar credential key is overwritten with a zod SafeParse result object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the whole `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed object, yet the result is stored directly: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)` returned the credential object. After the first token refresh the DB row becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in the constructor throws and the user's Google Calendar integration breaks permanently (requires reconnect). Either return `.data` from the helper or use `...data` here.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that evaluate to "[object Object]"
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed property names; a Zod schema object has no meaningful `toString()`, so both evaluate to the same literal key `"[object Object]"` and the second declaration overwrites the first. The effective schema is therefore `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`. Because Zod strips unknown keys by default, parsing a sync-endpoint response drops `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/`refresh_token` and everything else. Consumers (office365calendar, zoomvideo, salesforce) then persist a credential key containing only `access_token`, so the token is treated as permanently expired (or fails later schema validation) and a refresh is triggered on every call. The intent ("allow any extra properties, assume a numeric property is the expiry") needs `z.object({access_token: z.string()}).passthrough()` or `.catchall()`.

findings.title: Credential-sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect app-specific shapes
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `Response` of the POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, but several callers pass a `refreshFunction` whose return type is not a `Response`: hubspot's `tokensApi.createToken()` returns a token object and the caller reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` / `.accessToken`; zoho-bigin and zohocrm use axios and read `tokenInfo.data`; googlecalendar reads `res?.data`. With sync enabled these all read `undefined` off a `Response`, producing `NaN` expiry dates, `setAccessToken(undefined)` and corrupted credential rows instead of a working token. The helper needs to normalise the sync response to the same shape each caller expects (or each caller must branch explicitly).

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects a userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` – the third argument of the helper is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential id means the self-hosted endpoint is asked to refresh tokens for an unrelated (or non-existent) user, which at best fails and at worst returns another user's access token. `refreshAccessToken` only receives `credentialId`/`credentialKey`, so the credential's `userId` must be threaded through.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the refreshed-token response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This placeholder is then persisted into the credential key by callers (e.g. office365calendar, zoomvideo, salesforce). On the next refresh the provider is called with the bogus value `"refresh_token"`, which fails with invalid_grant and can mark the credential invalid — overwriting a previously valid refresh token with garbage. If the intent is "keep the existing refresh token", it must copy the old value from the stored credential instead of inventing a string.

findings.title: Salesforce now performs an unconditional token refresh on every service instantiation, and discards the new token
findings.body: `getClient()` unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token` each time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed — there is no expiry check as in the other apps. This burns Salesforce OAuth rate limits (and adds latency) on every booking operation. Worse, the refreshed token is written to the DB but the `jsforce.Connection` below is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the old token), so the refresh has no effect on the current request and an expired credential still fails.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh failure check relies on `response.statusText === "OK"`
findings.body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText })`. `statusText` is not guaranteed: HTTP/2 responses (which Salesforce serves) have an empty `statusText`, so a perfectly successful 200 response is rejected with an empty error message, and conversely error bodies are reported without any detail. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` and include the response body in the error.

findings.title: Webhook does not restrict HTTP method and crashes with 500 on malformed input
findings.body: The handler accepts any HTTP method (GET included) and calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without try/catch. A bad body, a wrong encryption key, or non-JSON plaintext throws out of the handler, returning an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400 with a useful message. Validate the method (POST only) and wrap parse/decrypt in error handling that returns 400.

findings.title: Updating a synced credential does not clear the `invalid` flag
findings.body: When an existing credential is found, only `key` is updated. If the credential had previously been marked `invalid: true` (which Cal.com does on invalid_grant, e.g. in googlecalendar/zoom/webex), pushing fresh working keys leaves `invalid` set, so the credential continues to be treated as broken and the app stays unusable for the user. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` (timing-unsafe) and header lookup is case-sensitive
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with a plain string inequality, which leaks information through timing; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]` relies on the operator setting the header name in lowercase (Node lowercases incoming header keys); if an uppercase name is configured the lookup silently returns `undefined` and every request is rejected with "Invalid webhook secret". Lowercase the configured name before the lookup.

findings.title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication and its status is not checked
findings.body: The POST to the self-hoster's credential sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret, signature or bearer token, so the endpoint handing out OAuth access tokens cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com and effectively has to be an unauthenticated public endpoint. (The inbound webhook does verify `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the outbound call should do the equivalent.) The response status is also never checked, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed downstream and parsed as if it were a token.

findings.title: Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo" which is not the app's slug
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug (used for `appId` in `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` and looked up by the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying their sync endpoint off the slug they receive from the webhook will not match the slug sent on refresh, so Zoom token refresh via credential sync silently fails. Other apps in this PR pass real slugs (e.g. `msteams`, `google-calendar`), so this is an inconsistency, not a convention.

findings.title: Webex refresh still validates with the strict schema, so credential sync responses are rejected
findings.body: Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but still parses the result with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `scope` to equal the exact literal `"spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write"`, plus `token_type`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. The documented sync-endpoint contract is "only the access token and expiry date", so with credential sharing enabled every Webex refresh rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". It should go through `parseRefreshTokenResponse` like zoom/office365/salesforce.

findings.title: No tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token-parsing helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that writes third-party OAuth credentials into the database plus two shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit or integration tests. Given the defects that are easy to introduce here (secret verification, decryption, schema shape, which branch of the helper is taken), tests covering: disabled sharing → 403, wrong secret → 403, unknown user/app → 404, create vs. update path, and the minimum-token-response parsing would prevent regressions in all app refresh flows.
